name: Wackernagel's Law
statement: Unstressed little words lean on the first word of a clause and settle into second position.
meaning: Wackernagel's law is the observation that in Proto-Indo-European and many of its daughter languages, and cross-linguistically, clitics, unstressed elements such as particles, pronouns, and auxiliaries, tend to occupy the second position in the clause, immediately after the first word or first constituent. Such elements are called second-position or Wackernagel clitics, and the slot they fill is the Wackernagel position. Because these little words cannot bear stress, they lean prosodically on the first stressed element and cannot themselves begin a sentence. Formulated by Jacob Wackernagel in 1892, the law is a foundational observation in the study of clitics and the prosody-syntax interface.
mechanism: Clitics are prosodically deficient: they cannot carry stress and form an accentual unit only in combination with a host. As a result they cannot stand at the start of a clause, where no host precedes them, and instead attach right after the first stressed word or first constituent, settling into second position. The first element carries the stress, and the unstressed clitics cluster behind it. Second position can be defined prosodically, after the first stressed word, or syntactically, after the first constituent, and languages differ in which they follow, which is one reason the law is a strong tendency rather than an absolute rule.

examples.text: The Latin enclitic -que, meaning and, attaches in second position, as in Senatus Populusque Romanus, the Senate and People of Rome, where -que leans on the preceding word.
Ancient Greek enclitic particles like te and the men-de pairing, and enclitic pronouns, characteristically occupy the second slot after the first word.
Serbo-Croatian and other South Slavic languages place clusters of pronominal and auxiliary clitics after the first stressed word or constituent, the classic modern Wackernagel system.

variants.name: Second word versus second constituent
variants.text: The ambiguity in defining second position, either prosodically after the first stressed word or syntactically after the first constituent, which languages resolve differently.

variants.name: Verb-adjacent clitics
variants.text: The contrasting pattern in some daughter languages where clitics attach to the verb rather than sitting in second position, showing not all clitics are Wackernagel clitics.

whyItMatters: Wackernagel's law is one of only a few generally accepted syntactic features reconstructed for Proto-Indo-European and its earliest descendants, and Wackernagel's 1892 essay was groundbreaking for both historical and theoretical linguistics. It is foundational to the study of clitics, word order, and the interface between prosody and syntax, and the term Wackernagel position is standard. It illuminates how unstressed elements find their place in a clause, connects the sound shape of words to their syntactic distribution, and remains a live topic wherever second-position clitic systems, such as those of the South Slavic languages, are studied.

working.text: expect unstressed clitics to appear right after the first word or constituent of a clause, in the Wackernagel position.
understand the placement as prosodic, since clitics cannot bear stress or begin a clause and must lean on a preceding host.
note whether a language counts second position after the first stressed word or after the first constituent, since the two can differ.

limits: Wackernagel's law is a strong tendency, not an exceptionless rule; it weakened or reshaped in many daughter languages and is best preserved today in the South Slavic clitic systems. Second position is genuinely ambiguous, defined either prosodically, after the first stressed word, or syntactically, after the first constituent, and languages differ in which they follow. Not all clitics are second-position, since some daughter languages have verb-adjacent clitics instead, and the law's application is neither uniform across Indo-European nor absolute within any one language.
misreadings: Second position does not always mean literally the second word, since it can mean after the first constituent, which may be several words long. It is a strong tendency, not an exceptionless law in the physical sense, and it weakened in many descendants. It does not apply uniformly to all clitics or all Indo-European languages, being best preserved in South Slavic today. And it should not be conflated with general second-position verb placement, a related but distinct phenomenon.
origin: Formulated by the Swiss Indo-Europeanist Jacob Wackernagel in his 1892 paper 'Über ein Gesetz der indogermanischen Wortstellung', on a law of Indo-European word order, in the journal Indogermanische Forschungen.

sources.text: Wackernagel's law, Wikipedia. — the second-position requirement, the prosodic motivation, and the Greek, Latin, and South Slavic examples.
Wackernagel, 'On a law of Indo-European word order' (1892), Language Science Press translation (2020). — the original statement of the law.
